**Answer: Yes, it is possible.**

**Proof.**

Let $p$ be a prime, and consider the field $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ of rational functions in one indeterminate $t$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$. This is the fraction field of the polynomial ring $\mathbb{F}_p[t]$.

**The field is infinite.** The elements $1, t, t^2, t^3, \dots$ are all distinct elements of $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$, so the field is infinite.

**Every element has finite additive order.** The field $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ has characteristic $p$, which means $p \cdot 1 = 0$ in the field. For any element $a \in \mathbb{F}_p(t)$, we compute:
$$p \cdot a = \underbrace{a + a + \cdots + a}_{p \text{ times}} = a \cdot \underbrace{(1 + 1 + \cdots + 1)}_{p \text{ times}} = a \cdot (p \cdot 1) = a \cdot 0 = 0.$$
Thus every element $a$ satisfies $p \cdot a = 0$, so the additive order of every element divides $p$ and is therefore finite (it is $1$ for $a = 0$, and exactly $p$ for $a \neq 0$, since no smaller positive multiple of a nonzero element can vanish in characteristic $p$).

Hence $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ is an infinite field in which every element has finite additive order. $\blacksquare$
